name: Claude Monet
bio: A founder of Impressionism, whose Impression, Sunrise gave the movement its name, Monet painted outdoors to catch the changing light on water, fields and gardens. In his garden at Giverny he painted his water lilies again and again for the last decades of his life.

name: Rembrandt van Rijn
bio: The greatest painter of the Dutch Golden Age, Rembrandt used deep shadow and warm light to show the inner life of his sitters. He made dozens of self-portraits, from youth to old age.

name: Artemisia Gentileschi
bio: Artemisia was the daughter of a painter and showed incredible skill from a young age. She was the first woman to become a member of the Accademia di Arte del Disegno in Florence. Influenced by Caravaggio’s use of chiaroscuro, she painted arresting images of intensely lifelike human figures, often featured as strong heroines from the Bible and historical events.

name: Peter Paul Rubens
bio: The leading painter of the Flemish Baroque, Rubens filled huge canvases with movement, rich colour and energetic figures. He was also a diplomat, sent on missions between the royal courts of Europe.

name: Caravaggio
bio: Caravaggio thrilled and shocked Rome with true-to-life people lit by a dramatic spotlight against dark backgrounds. His strong contrast of light and shadow shaped Baroque painting across Europe.

name: Vincent van Gogh
bio: A Dutch Post-Impressionist, Vincent van Gogh painted for only about ten years, yet his bold colour and thick, swirling brushstrokes changed modern art. He sold almost nothing in his lifetime and is now one of the best-loved painters in the world.

name: El Greco
bio: Born on Crete and trained in Venice, El Greco settled in Toledo, Spain. His long, flickering figures and strange, intense colours belong to the late Renaissance style called Mannerism.

name: Titian
bio: The greatest painter of Renaissance Venice, Titian was famous for rich colour and free, loose brushwork. Kings and popes sat for his portraits, and he went on painting for more than sixty years.

name: Raphael
bio: With Leonardo and Michelangelo, Raphael was one of the three great masters of the High Renaissance. He was famous for calm, graceful Madonnas and for the frescoes he painted in the Pope’s rooms in the Vatican.

name: Berthe Morisot
bio: A founding member of the Impressionist group, Morisot showed in all but one of its eight exhibitions. She painted women and children at home and in gardens with quick, feathery brushstrokes.

name: Leonardo da Vinci
bio: The great all-round genius of the Italian Renaissance, Leonardo was a painter, inventor, engineer and student of the human body. He finished few paintings, but they include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

name: Mary Cassatt
bio: An American who spent most of her life in Paris, Cassatt was the only American to exhibit with the Impressionists. She is best known for her tender pictures of mothers and children.

name: Sandro Botticelli
bio: A Florentine painter of the Early Renaissance, Botticelli worked for the Medici family and painted graceful figures with flowing lines. He is best known for The Birth of Venus and Primavera.

name: Paul Cézanne
bio: A French Post-Impressionist, Cézanne built his pictures from patches of colour, looking for the solid shapes beneath nature. Picasso and the Cubists saw him as the father of modern art.

name: Edgar Degas
bio: Degas showed with the Impressionists but called himself a realist, preferring the studio to painting outdoors. He is famous for ballet dancers, racehorses and everyday Paris life seen from unusual angles.

name: Edouard Manet
bio: Manet painted modern Paris in bold, flat colour, and his daring pictures shocked the official art world. The young Impressionists looked to him as their leader, though he never showed in their exhibitions.

name: Paul Gauguin
bio: A Post-Impressionist who began as a stockbroker, Gauguin painted in flat areas of bold colour, first in Brittany and later in Tahiti. He looked to folk art and faraway places for a simpler way of seeing.

name: Auguste Renoir
bio: A leading Impressionist who began as a painter of porcelain, Renoir loved to paint people enjoying themselves: dances, boating parties, women and children, all in warm, feathery colour.

name: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
bio: Toulouse-Lautrec painted the nightlife of Montmartre in Paris, its dancers, singers and cafés, with quick, lively lines. His bold posters for the Moulin Rouge helped make the poster an art form.

name: Auguste Rodin
bio: The most famous sculptor of his time, Rodin modelled bodies full of movement and feeling, as in The Thinker and The Kiss. His rough, expressive surfaces opened the way to modern sculpture.

name: Edwin Landseer
bio: Victorian Britain's best-loved animal painter and a favourite of Queen Victoria, Landseer gave the Romantic love of the Scottish Highlands its stags and noble dogs. He also modelled the bronze lions in Trafalgar Square.

name: Hudson River School
bio: Not one painter but a group of American landscape artists, led by Thomas Cole, who painted the wild valleys and mountains of New York and New England. Their grand, glowing views share the Romantic sense of nature as awe-inspiring and sacred.

name: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot
bio: A bridge between Romantic landscape and Impressionism, Corot painted outdoors in France and Italy and is loved for the silvery, misty landscapes of his later years. The young Impressionists looked to him as a master.

name: Camille Pissarro
bio: The oldest of the Impressionists, and the only one to show in all eight of their exhibitions, Pissarro painted farms, villages and later busy city streets. He was a generous teacher to the younger Cézanne and Gauguin.

name: Joseph DeCamp
bio: A Boston painter and a member of the Ten American Painters, a group of American Impressionists, DeCamp painted calm, light-filled rooms with women reading, sewing or playing music.

name: John Everett Millais
bio: A child prodigy and a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, Millais painted early works such as Ophelia in astonishing detail. He went on to become one of the most successful painters in Victorian Britain.

name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
bio: Poet as well as painter, Rossetti was a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848. His later pictures of dreamy women with flowing hair and rich colour helped shape the Aesthetic Movement.

name: William Holman Hunt
bio: A founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848, Hunt kept to its ideals of sharp detail and bright, natural colour all his life. He travelled to the Holy Land to paint Bible scenes where they took place.

name: Ford Madox Brown
bio: An older friend of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood rather than a member, Brown shared its bright colour and close detail. He is best known for scenes of modern life, such as emigrants leaving England in The Last of England.

name: Arthur Hughes
bio: Drawn to the Pre-Raphaelites as a young man, Hughes painted tender scenes of love and longing, famous for their glowing purples and greens. He also illustrated many books for children.

name: Edward Burne-Jones
bio: A leader of the second wave of the Pre-Raphaelites, Burne-Jones painted dreamlike scenes from myth and legend in soft, glowing colour. He worked with his friend William Morris on stained glass, tapestries and books.

name: Marie Spartali Stillman
bio: One of the few women painters among the Pre-Raphaelites, Stillman studied with Ford Madox Brown and modelled for Rossetti. She painted scenes from Italian poetry and legend in soft watercolour.

name: Evelyn De Morgan
bio: A later Pre-Raphaelite inspired by Burne-Jones and the Italian Renaissance, De Morgan filled her pictures with allegorical figures in rich, jewel-like colour. She used myth to speak of the spirit, of war and of the rights of women.

name: John William Waterhouse
bio: Working a generation after the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, Waterhouse painted women of myth and legend, like the Lady of Shalott, in a softer, looser style. He is often called the last Pre-Raphaelite.

name: Edward Robert Hughes
bio: Nephew of Arthur Hughes and assistant to William Holman Hunt, he carried the Pre-Raphaelite style into the twentieth century. He was a master of watercolour, painting fairies, twilight and magic.

name: Joseph Noel Paton
bio: A Scottish painter close to the Pre-Raphaelites, Paton is best known for his fairy scenes from Shakespeare, crowded with tiny figures. In later life he turned to religious subjects.

name: Frederick Sandys
bio: A painter from Norwich in Rossetti's circle, Sandys was admired for his precise drawing and jewel-bright detail. His sorceresses and legendary queens are among the most striking Pre-Raphaelite portraits.

name: John Brett
bio: Brett began as a Pre-Raphaelite, painting every stone and leaf with near-scientific precision, encouraged by the critic John Ruskin. A keen astronomer too, he later turned to wide, glittering seascapes of the British coast.

name: Sophie Gengembre Anderson
bio: Born in Paris and settled in England, Anderson painted sweet, finely finished pictures of children and young women, close in spirit to the Pre-Raphaelites. She lived for years on the island of Capri, whose light and people fill much of her work.

name: Frederic Leighton
bio: The leading figure of Victorian Classicism, Leighton painted graceful scenes of ancient Greece and Rome in warm, glowing colour. He was the first painter to be made a lord.
